## OB-001 Goal Hijacking

Actors use adversarial instructions and context manipulation to override, bypass, alter, or subvert an LLM/agent's system instructions, guardrails, or intended behavior. This objective encapsulates prompt injection and jailbreak-style attacks, including direct user prompting, indirect payload delivery through external content, multimodal payloads, and multi-turn goal drift. The attack manipulates model context so the system follows attacker-controlled objectives instead of aligned constraints.

### AITech-1.1 Direct Prompt Injection and Jailbreak (Prompt-based Manipulation)

Text-based prompt techniques to manipulate an LLM/agent's behavior to bypass safeguards and/or follow attacker-defined goals. This can include the use of obfuscation, context and instruction manipulation, or propagating attacks through multi-agent environments.

| Sub-technique | Name | Definition |
|---|---|---|
| `AISubtech-1.1.1` | Instruction Manipulation | Attempts to override, replace, or reprioritize system directives so the model follows attacker-controlled instructions. |
| `AISubtech-1.1.2` | Obfuscation | Disguising malicious payload intent with encoding, formatting, language tricks, or paraphrase chains to evade guardrails. |
| `AISubtech-1.1.3` | Multi-Agent Propagation | Propagating malicious instructions across agent boundaries so downstream agents trust and execute attacker objectives. |
| `AISubtech-1.1.4` | Token Exploitation | Exploiting tokenization, control-sequence, parser, or delimiter edge cases to trigger unsafe handling or bypass controls. |
| `AISubtech-1.1.5` | Context Manipulation | Using fabricated framing -- through roleplay, staged scenarios, false premises, or adversarial argumentation -- to make harmful outputs appear permissible. |

### AITech-1.2 Indirect Prompt Injection

Variation of prompt-based manipulation where the attacker embeds malicious instructions in external data sources (such as web pages, documents, emails, databases, API responses, etc.) that the LLM or the agent retrieves and processes, causing attacker instructions to be executed. The attack exploits the model's inability to distinguish between trusted system instructions and untrusted external content.

This technique has no sub-techniques.

### AITech-1.3 Multimodal Injection and Manipulation

Actors deliberately insert, alter, or create malicious content across various modalities (such as text, image, audio, video, or sensor streams) to influence, corrupt, or exploit an AI system's fusion, interpretation, or decision-making processes. Attacks exploit the integration points where different data types are combined.

| Sub-technique | Name | Definition |
|---|---|---|
| `AISubtech-1.3.1` | Image-Text Injection | Embedding malicious instructions, prompts, or data within images using techniques such as steganography, adversarial stickers, embedded text, or visual triggers. These elements are often imperceptible to humans but are extracted, interpreted, or acted upon by vision language models or downstream agents. The image serves as a carrier for a linguistic or symbolic payload intended to influence model behavior. |
| `AISubtech-1.3.2` | Image Manipulation | Modifying visual content across any modality by altering pixels, structure, or image features to influence model perception or decision-making. This includes adding noise, applying transformations, overlaying patterns or text, or generating multiple manipulated variants to exploit weaknesses in vision encoders, robustness layers, or safety filters. The manipulation targets how the model interprets the image itself rather than embedding hidden instructions. |
| `AISubtech-1.3.3` | Audio Command Injection | Hidden, inaudible, or unintelligible voice commands and instructions embedded in audio streams using ultrasonic frequencies, backmasking, or steganographic techniques that automatic speech recognition (ASR) models interpret as valid instructions. |
| `AISubtech-1.3.4` | Video Overlay Manipulation | Embedding harmful content or malicious instructions in video streams through specific frames, QR-like triggers, or temporal injection that misleads multimodal model perception and bypasses guardrails or defensive measures. |

## OB-002 Agentic Autonomy Failures (Misuse, Alignment, Drift)

External actors or the agent itself (in cases of autonomy failure) cause behavior to diverge from the user or organization's authorized intent and scope. That drift happens in the agent's authorized capabilities, trust in its own assets and channels, attempts to optimize against success metrics or scores instead of the user's goal, and chained authority in composed workflows. This objective covers an agent's failures to select, scope, verify, and optimize tasks within its own action space.

### AITech-2.1 Excessive Agency

External actors or the agent itself leverage the agent's authorized capabilities, available tools, lack of oversight on consequential actions, or interpretive drift across turns to commit to an action that exceeds its authorized decision-making, scope, or execution authority.

| Sub-technique | Name | Definition |
|---|---|---|
| `AISubtech-2.1.1` | Execution Approval Bypass | The agent performs, attempts, schedules, submits, or makes a concrete operational commitment to a consequential action for which the visible governing contract requires explicit, current approval, without obtaining valid approval for that action. This includes acting before approval, treating silence or ambiguous language as approval, reusing approval from a different action, or manufacturing urgency to bypass review. |
| `AISubtech-2.1.2` | Capability and Permission Overreach | The agent uses or commits to a capability, permission, resource, target, or operation outside visible current task authority, even when the agent technically possesses the access. The agent may remain within its technically assigned credentials while exceeding task-level authority, such as modifying data when only inspection was requested or operating on a broader set of targets than authorized. |

### AITech-2.2 Goal Drift

The agent independently and materially expands, refuses, substitutes, or abandons the governing objective, authorized scope, or material constraints. The drift is in the agent's interpretation of authorized scope, including overreaching tasks in an attempt to be helpful, reframing tasks it can't satisfy to a task it can satisfy, gaining access to tools by approvals from the user over multi-turn sessions even if task scope changes, and breaking rules such as violating environmental boundaries to complete tasks.

| Sub-technique | Name | Definition |
|---|---|---|
| `AISubtech-2.2.1` | Unauthorized Scope Expansion | The agent independently retains the governing objective but later adds agent-originated material tasks, targets, systems, people, permissions, or consequential actions outside its authorized scope. The expansion is commonly justified as necessary, helpful, preventative, or implied by the original request. |
| `AISubtech-2.2.2` | Goal Substitution | The agent visibly and without a supported basis refuses, rejects, or abandons the applicable governing objective, or adopts an easier, adjacent, available, or self-selected operative objective or success condition in its place. It may complete a proxy task, provide an adjacent deliverable, or redefine success and then represent that substituted outcome as fulfillment of the original task. |
| `AISubtech-2.2.3` | Authorization and Constraint Erosion | The agent independently weakens, reinterprets, ignores, or discards an observable governing constraint during execution. This includes treating prior approvals as durable authority, converting hard boundaries into preferences, carrying exceptions into unrelated tasks, or abandoning environmental and policy constraints to complete the task. |

### AITech-2.3 Reward Hacking

External actors or autonomy failure cause the agent to optimize observable success signals--test pass/fail, benchmark scores, verifier outputs, approval heuristics, cost/latency budgets, dashboard metrics--instead of the visible governing task or objective. The agent seeks, obtains, claims, or preserves apparent success while exploiting task or interface mismatches, subverting verification, taking invalidating shortcuts, or degrading measurement integrity. Deliberate acquisition of an invalidating shortcut for task advantage can qualify before it is used in a result.

| Sub-technique | Name | Definition |
|---|---|---|
| `AISubtech-2.3.1` | Task Loophole Exploitation | The agent exploits a loophole or mismatch in the task, environment, interface, or success criteria so apparent success is obtained or claimed while a material task requirement remains unmet. |
| `AISubtech-2.3.2` | Verifier Manipulation | The agent alters, disables, bypasses, selectively invokes, or manipulates tests, graders, approval checks, monitoring, logs, or validation inputs and outputs so that an unsuccessful or unsafe result is recorded as successful. Examples include weakening assertions, suppressing failures, modifying evaluation configuration, or fabricating completion evidence. |
| `AISubtech-2.3.3` | Shortcut Acquisition | The agent obtains answers, completion artifacts, or privileged solution information through prohibited or measurement-invalidating channels instead of performing the intended task. Examples include accessing answer keys, leaked benchmark data, newer fixed code, hidden reference artifacts, cached outputs, or published challenge solutions. |

## OB-003 Masquerading / Obfuscation / Impersonation

Actors introduce a malicious agent that impersonates a legitimate agent, user, system, or authority within a multi-agent ecosystem and causes other agents, systems, or users to accept it as authentic and trust its communications or actions.

### AITech-3.1 Masquerading / Obfuscation / Impersonation

Actors introduce a malicious agent that impersonates a legitimate agent, user, system, or authority within a multi-agent ecosystem and causes other agents, systems, or users to accept it as authentic and trust its communications or actions.

| Sub-technique | Name | Definition |
|---|---|---|
| `AISubtech-3.1.1` | Identity Obfuscation | Manipulating agent or user identity representation within context, metadata, or interaction patterns to evade detection, tracking, or access controls. |
| `AISubtech-3.1.2` | Trusted Agent Spoofing | Masquerading as a legitimate agent or MCP-registered service to inject malicious instructions, responses, or outputs that other agents, services, or users treat as trusted. This attack exploits the assumption of authenticity within multi-agent systems and protocol-mediated toolchains, enabling actors to bypass safeguards and influence downstream behavior. |

## OB-004 Communication Compromise

Actors manipulate an agent system to introduce or executive unaothorized agent instances, malicious agent code, or fake agent capabilities by inserting misleading data, exploiting registration mechanisms, or subverting agent deployment processes. This results in unauthorized agents operating within the system or legitimate agents executing malicious code.

### AITech-4.1 Agent Injection

Actors manipulate an agent system to introduce or executive unauthorized agent instances, malicious agent code, or fake agent capabilities by inserting misleading data, exploiting registration mechanisms, or subverting agent deployment processes. This results in unauthorized agents operating within the system or legitimate agents executing malicious code.

| Sub-technique | Name | Definition |
|---|---|---|
| `AISubtech-4.1.1` | Rogue Agent Introduction | Unauthorized insertion of a malicious agent into a multi-agent system that operates contrary to intended purpose, designed to steal data, cause disruption, or autonomously serve attacker goals while exploiting legitimate access patterns or mimicking normal behavior to evade detection. |

### AITech-4.2 Context Boundary Attacks

Actors manipulate contextual information that an agent sees, processes, or transmits by exploiting unclear or porous boundaries between different context segments (such as descriptions, prompts, tool outputs, memory, or status messages). An agent may misinterpret the source, trustworthiness, or intent of information.

| Sub-technique | Name | Definition |
|---|---|---|
| `AISubtech-4.2.1` | Context Window Exploitation | Deliberate overloading or manipulation of the limited context window of a model/agent to displace, overwrite, or push out crucial system instructions or safety guidelines with attacker-supplied text. |
| `AISubtech-4.2.2` | Session Boundary Violation | Crossing expected conversational or transactional boundaries to persist malicious instructions, adversarial content, or misleading data across separate sessions through exploitation of persistent memory, session management flaws, or memory carryover mechanisms. |

### AITech-4.3 Protocol Manipulation

Actors exploit assumptions or ambiguities in structured communication protocols (e.g., JSON, XML, YAML, API specifications, custom schemas) used for agentic communication by introducing adversarial inputs that corrupt parsing, processing, or interpretation.

| Sub-technique | Name | Definition |
|---|---|---|
| `AISubtech-4.3.1` | Schema Inconsistencies | Exploiting irregular, conflicting, or misaligned data structure, format, or organization that doesn't align with model expectations, and can result in vulnerabilities, model performance degradation, parsing errors, or security bypasses. |
| `AISubtech-4.3.2` | Namespace Collision | Exploited situation where two or more components (e.g., datasets, variables, functions, APIs, tools, or model identifiers) share the same name or identifier, resulting in confusion, misrouting, or security vulnerabilities in AI systems. |
| `AISubtech-4.3.3` | Server Rebinding Attack | Exploiting DNS rebinding or similar techniques to confuse an AI model or agent into treating an external, attacker-controlled domain as if it were part of the trusted internal network, bypassing same-origin policies and network security controls. |
| `AISubtech-4.3.4` | Replay Exploitation | Capturing legitimate requests, communications, API calls, model queries, or authentication tokens to an AI system and resending (replaying) them later to trick the system into performing the same action again or bypassing authentication. |
| `AISubtech-4.3.5` | Capability Inflation | Exploiting system mechanisms to artificially expand, escalate, or misrepresent an agent's, model's, or component's capabilities, permissions, or authority beyond intended limits, enabling unauthorized actions or access. |
| `AISubtech-4.3.6` | Cross-Origin Exploitation | Subverting security mechanisms designed to isolate web resources, primarily the Same-Origin Policy (SOP), within an AI agent's architecture in order to trick the AI agent or its execution environment into making unauthorized requests, sharing sensitive data, or executing actions across different trust boundaries (e.g., distinct domains, protocols, or services). |

## OB-005 Persistence

Actors insert poisoned, harmful, or adversarial data or instructions into an agent or model's short-term or long-term memory to corrupt its behavior over extended periods of time.

### AITech-5.1 Memory System Persistence

Actors insert poisoned, harmful, or adversarial data or instructions into an agent or model's short-term or long-term memory to corrupt its behavior over extended periods of time.

| Sub-technique | Name | Definition |
|---|---|---|
| `AISubtech-5.1.1` | Long-term / Short-term Memory Injection | Seeding malicious, misleading, or adversarial data into an LLM's or agent's persistent memory (long-term) or working memory (short-term) to influence current and future interactions, bias behavior, or enable persistent attacks. |

### AITech-5.2 Configuration Persistence

Actor subverts an agent's internal configuration, settings, or initialization parameters to create lasting malicious influence over its behavior. This goes beyond a single, isolated prompt injection by modifying the system's core settings, context, or memory that defines its behavior. An example is modifying MCP configuration to include a malicious server or inserting malicious instructions into an integrated development environment's internal config files.

| Sub-technique | Name | Definition |
|---|---|---|
| `AISubtech-5.2.1` | Agent Profile Tampering | Unauthorized alteration of stored agent identity, preferences, role definitions, capabilities, permissions, or behavioral parameters to enable malicious behaviors, persist access, escalate privileges, or evade detection. |

## OB-006 Feedback Loop Manipulation

Actors insert malicious, inaccurate, or corrupted data into a model's training pipeline, with the aim of distorting the model's outputs, embedding payload, degrading performance, or introducing systematic biases.

### AITech-6.1 Training Data Poisoning

Actors insert malicious, inaccurate, or corrupted data into a model's training pipeline, with the aim of distorting the model's outputs, embedding payload, degrading performance, or introducing systematic biases.

| Sub-technique | Name | Definition |
|---|---|---|
| `AISubtech-6.1.1` | Knowledge Base Poisoning | Inserting false, malicious, biased, or misleading data into external knowledge bases, vector databases, or RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation) systems that LLMs or agents rely on for responses, corrupting outputs and decisions. |
| `AISubtech-6.1.2` | Reinforcement Biasing | Subtly influencing user feedback, evaluation signals, or reward mechanisms in reinforcement learning systems to skew the learning process toward attacker goals, shifting intended model behavior. |
| `AISubtech-6.1.3` | Reinforcement Signal Corruption | Directly injecting false, adversarial, or manipulated signals into training pipelines, feedback channels, or reward systems to actively degrade model performance or subvert learning objectives through reward hacking. |

## OB-007 Sabotage / Integrity Degradation

Actors subvert a model/agent's planning, decision-making, or logical inference processes to produce unintended or harmful outcomes. As AI agents are increasingly trusted with autonomous actions, this attack targets the agent's "reasoning engine" i.e, the core mechanisms for analysis, judgment, and action selection.

### AITech-7.1 Reasoning Corruption

Actors subvert a model/agent's planning, decision-making, or logical inference processes to produce unintended or harmful outcomes. As AI agents are increasingly trusted with autonomous actions, this attack targets the agent's "reasoning engine" i.e, the core mechanisms for analysis, judgment, and action selection.

This technique has no sub-techniques.

### AITech-7.2 Memory System Corruption

Actors inject false, malicious, or adversarial data into an AI agent's memory systems to cause immediate harmful decisions, corruption of system functionality or degraded performance.

| Sub-technique | Name | Definition |
|---|---|---|
| `AISubtech-7.2.1` | Memory Anchor Attacks | Strategically planting memorable or salient content to bias the model/agent's recall toward attacker-chosen information. |
| `AISubtech-7.2.2` | Memory Index Manipulation | Altering how memory embeddings, indexes, or retrieval mechanisms are generated, stored, or queried to favor retrieval of attacker-controlled content over legitimate information. |

### AITech-7.3 Data Source Abuse and Manipulation

Actors inject malicious, misleading, or poisoned data into external data sources (APIs, databases, RAG systems) that AI systems consume in order to manipulate model behavior, corrupt decision-making, or inject malicious instructions through trusted data channels.

| Sub-technique | Name | Definition |
|---|---|---|
| `AISubtech-7.3.1` | Corrupted Third-Party Data | External datasets from vendors, partners, open-source repositories, or public sources containing inaccurate, incomplete, malicious, or manipulated information that is used in training, fine-tuning, or evaluating an AI model. |

### AITech-7.4 Token Manipulation

Actors misuse, poison, or tamper with tokens used by model/agentic systems (e.g., model-specific tokens, or security tokens) to control access, encode information, or manage interactions.

| Sub-technique | Name | Definition |
|---|---|---|
| `AISubtech-7.4.1` | Token Theft | Actors steal authentication tokens, API keys, or credentials from Model Context Protocol servers or similar agent-integration frameworks to gain unauthorized access to connected systems, impersonate legitimate agents, or access restricted resources. |

## OB-008 Data and Privacy Violations

Actors expose, infer, extract, generate, or misuse sensitive, personal, financial, health, proprietary, or system information through model outputs, training data analysis, agent tooling, or system interactions. This objective covers unauthorized disclosure of training data, prompts and metadata, personally identifiable information, payment card industry data, and protected health information to parties who should not have access.

### AITech-8.1 Membership Inference

Actors determine whether a specific data point, record, or individual was included in a model's training dataset, exposing sensitive information about training data subjects, reveal proprietary datasets, or indicate the presence of confidential information in model training.

| Sub-technique | Name | Definition |
|---|---|---|
| `AISubtech-8.1.1` | Presence Detection | Querying and verifying whether a specific datapoint, record, or piece of information was present in the training dataset, knowledge base, or system memory through targeted queries and behavioral analysis. |

### AITech-8.2 Data Exfiltration / Exposure

Actors intentionally or unintentionally cause sensitive information to be exposed through model outputs, API responses, or system behaviors. This includes leakage of personal data, intellectual property, proprietary algorithms, training data, system internals, or other confidential information to unauthorized parties.

| Sub-technique | Name | Definition |
|---|---|---|
| `AISubtech-8.2.1` | Training Data Exposure | Information contained in the dataset used to train and maintain an AI model can be retrieved, reconstructed, or inferred from the model's outputs, internal behavior, or responses, violating privacy of training data subjects. |
| `AISubtech-8.2.2` | LLM Data Leakage | The release of sensitive or personally identifiable information (PII) from its training data during inference through prompt injection or other extraction techniques. |
| `AISubtech-8.2.3` | Data Exfiltration via Agent Tooling | Unintentional and/or unauthorized exposure or exfiltration of sensitive information, such as private or sensitive data, intellectual property, and proprietary algorithms through exploitation of agent tools, integrations, or capabilities, where the agent is manipulated to use legitimate tools for malicious data exfiltration purposes. |

### AITech-8.3 Information Disclosure

Actors trigger the unintentional or unauthorized exposure, leakage, or sharing of data, model parameters, or system details to parties who should not have access to them. The disclosure occurs through model behaviors, responses, or system interactions that reveal more information than intended.

| Sub-technique | Name | Definition |
|---|---|---|
| `AISubtech-8.3.1` | Tool Metadata Exposure | Disclosure of non-functional descriptive data about tools (names, descriptions, parameter schemas, versions, capabilities) that attackers can use to manipulate tool selection or agent behavior. |
| `AISubtech-8.3.2` | System Information Leakage | Unintended disclosure of internal configuration, architecture, environment details, system-level variables (OS, file paths, hardware, network), or infrastructure information that aids attackers in crafting attacks or gaining unauthorized access. |

### AITech-8.4 Prompt/Meta Extraction

Actors extract, reveal, or reconstruct the system prompts, meta-prompts, hidden instructions, initial context, or operational directives that define a model/agent's behavior, constraints, and capabilities. This can expose intellectual property, security mechanisms, and operational logic.

| Sub-technique | Name | Definition |
|---|---|---|
| `AISubtech-8.4.1` | System LLM Prompt Leakage | Exposure of system prompts, instructions, or initial context used to steer model behavior, potentially revealing sensitive information, security mechanisms, intellectual property, or operational details not intended for discovery. |

### AITech-8.5 Personally Identifiable Information

Exposure, generation, or misuse of personally identifiable information (PII) such as names, addresses, phone numbers, identification numbers, or other sensitive personal details that can be used to identify, track, or exploit individuals.

| Sub-technique | Name | Definition |
|---|---|---|
| `AISubtech-8.5.1` | Email Address | Exposure or generation of email addresses. |
| `AISubtech-8.5.2` | Phone Number | Exposure or generation of phone numbers. |
| `AISubtech-8.5.3` | Person Name | Exposure or generation of individual person names. |
| `AISubtech-8.5.4` | IP Address | Exposure or generation of IP addresses. |
| `AISubtech-8.5.5` | Address | Exposure or generation of physical/mailing addresses. |
| `AISubtech-8.5.6` | Username | Exposure or generation of usernames. |
| `AISubtech-8.5.7` | Password | Exposure or generation of passwords or credential material. |
| `AISubtech-8.5.8` | Driver License Number | Exposure or generation of driver license numbers. |
| `AISubtech-8.5.9` | Passport Number | Exposure or generation of passport numbers. |
| `AISubtech-8.5.10` | National ID Number | Exposure or generation of national identification numbers (e.g., SSN, national insurance number). |

### AITech-8.6 Payment Card Industry Data

Exposure, generation, or misuse of payment card industry (PCI) data including cardholder data and sensitive authentication data such as card numbers, expiration dates, service codes, CVVs, and PINs.

| Sub-technique | Name | Definition |
|---|---|---|
| `AISubtech-8.6.1` | Credit Card Number | Exposure or generation of credit card numbers (primary account numbers). |
| `AISubtech-8.6.2` | Bank Account Number | Exposure or generation of bank account numbers. |
| `AISubtech-8.6.3` | Bank Routing Code | Exposure or generation of bank routing codes or sort codes. |
| `AISubtech-8.6.4` | Tax Identification Number | Exposure or generation of tax identification numbers (e.g., EIN, TIN). |

### AITech-8.7 Protected Health Information

Exposure, generation, or misuse of protected health information (PHI) including individually identifiable health data such as medical records, diagnoses, billing information, and other personal health identifiers.

| Sub-technique | Name | Definition |
|---|---|---|
| `AISubtech-8.7.1` | Medical License Number | Exposure or generation of medical license numbers. |
| `AISubtech-8.7.2` | Patient ID Number | Exposure or generation of patient identification numbers. |
| `AISubtech-8.7.3` | Medication | Exposure or generation of medication information linked to identifiable individuals. |
| `AISubtech-8.7.4` | Medical Disease | Exposure or generation of disease or diagnosis information linked to identifiable individuals. |

## OB-009 Supply Chain Compromise

Actor coerces or manipulates a model/agent into producing false, misleading or malicious outputs through adversarial inputs, context manipulation, or exploiting model behaviors, without directly modifying the model itself.

### AITech-9.1 Model or Agentic System Manipulation

Actor coerces or manipulates a model/agent into producing false, misleading or malicious outputs through adversarial inputs, context manipulation, or exploiting model behaviors, without directly modifying the model itself.

| Sub-technique | Name | Definition |
|---|---|---|
| `AISubtech-9.1.1` | Code Execution | Exploitation of AI models equipped with code interpreter tools that can autonomously write, test, and execute code, enabling attackers to run arbitrary code on the underlying system through prompt injection or tool manipulation. |
| `AISubtech-9.1.2` | Unauthorized or Unsolicited System Access | Manipulating or accessing underlying system resources without authorization, leading to unsolicited modification or deletion of files, configurations, or permissions, and enabling system-level command execution on the host. Such activity may result in privilege escalation, file tampering, or unauthorized control over infrastructure through model-driven, agent-executed, or automated system interactions. |
| `AISubtech-9.1.3` | Unauthorized or Unsolicited Network Access | Exploiting models or agents to gain unauthorized access to network resources, internal systems, external services, or restricted network segments through model-driven requests, agent capabilities, or network tool exploitation. |
| `AISubtech-9.1.4` | Injection Attacks (e.g., SQL, Command Execution, XSS) | Leveraging an LLM to generate, optimize, or automatically adapt injection payloads that bypass detection mechanisms or exploit system vulnerabilities. The LLM/agent acts as an intermediary tool that crafts, refines, or personalizes the malicious injection. |
| `AISubtech-9.1.5` | Template Injection (e.g., SSTI) | Manipulating a template engine by injecting malicious syntax, expressions, or code into a data field that is later rendered or processed. Model output is unsafely embedded into a server-side template (e.g., using Jinja2, Handlebars, or Mustache) allowing the attacker to execute arbitrary code, manipulate template logic, or compromise the underlying system. |

### AITech-9.2 Detection Evasion

Actors manipulate or alter the input data, behaviors, or attack patterns to intentionally bypass security monitoring, content moderation, anomaly detection, and safety mechanisms.

| Sub-technique | Name | Definition |
|---|---|---|
| `AISubtech-9.2.1` | Obfuscation Vulnerabilities | Weaknesses that emerge when parts of the AI system (code, model architecture, parameters, configurations) are intentionally or unintentionally concealed or obscured, creating security blind spots and attack opportunities. |
| `AISubtech-9.2.2` | Backdoors and Trojans | A model that has been maliciously modified to exhibit trigger-activated behavior (i.e., misclassification, malicious outputs, undesirable biases in responses) when given specific inputs, but behaves normally otherwise. |

### AITech-9.3 Dependency / Plugin Compromise

Actors insert malicious code, backdoors, or vulnerabilities into third-party dependencies, plugins, extensions, or libraries used by models/agents/AI applications, creating supply chain attacks that affect all systems using the compromised component.

| Sub-technique | Name | Definition |
|---|---|---|
| `AISubtech-9.3.1` | Malicious Package / Tool Injection | Introduction of malicious or adversarial tools, APIs, or packages into the toolset, registry, or dependency chain used by a system or agent, enabling the model to unknowingly invoke compromised tools that can execute attacks or expose data. |
| `AISubtech-9.3.2` | Dependency Name Squatting (Tools / Servers) | Publishing malicious packages, tools, or MCP servers with names similar to legitimate ones (typosquatting, combosquatting) to trick developers, orchestrators, or agents into installing and using compromised components. |
| `AISubtech-9.3.3` | Dependency Replacement / Rug Pull | Replacing a once-legitimate, trusted tool, package, or server with malicious code after trust and adoption have been established, exploiting existing deployments that auto-update. |

## OB-010 Model Theft / Extraction

Actors attempt to reconstruct or replicate a model partially or entirely by interacting with it through its APIs, inference endpoints, or other access points, with the goal of replicating its functionality, architecture, parameters, or outputs without authorized access.

### AITech-10.1 Model Extraction

Actors attempt to reconstruct or replicate a model partially or entirely by interacting with it through its APIs, inference endpoints, or other access points, with the goal of replicating its functionality, architecture, parameters, or outputs without authorized access.

| Sub-technique | Name | Definition |
|---|---|---|
| `AISubtech-10.1.1` | API Query Stealing | Sending systematic requests to an AI model's API to extract responses, behavior patterns, or model characteristics without proper authorization, building a dataset to replicate model functionality. |
| `AISubtech-10.1.2` | Weight Reconstruction | Attempts to recover or approximate underlying weights, parameters, or model architecture of a trained model, by exploiting access to the model's outputs, API queries or side channels. |
| `AISubtech-10.1.3` | Sensitive Data Reconstruction | Reconstructing sensitive datasets, personally identifiable information (PII), or training data from a model's outputs through targeted queries, model inversion attacks, or memorization exploitation. |

### AITech-10.2 Model Inversion

Actors reconstructs private training data, sensitive features, or confidential information from a trained model by exploiting the model's learned representations, decision boundaries, or output patterns.

| Sub-technique | Name | Definition |
|---|---|---|
| `AISubtech-10.2.1` | Model Inversion | Actors reconstructs private training data, sensitive features, or confidential information from a trained model by exploiting the model's learned representations, decision boundaries, or output patterns. |

## OB-011 Adversarial Evasion

Actors manipulate the model by exploiting aspects of its operational context, or "environment," to induce malicious or unintended behavior. Rather than simply altering a user's prompt, this type of attack crafts input to leverage the system's broader state and external interactions to bypass safety measures.

### AITech-11.1 Environment-Aware Evasion

Actors manipulate the model by exploiting aspects of its operational context, or "environment," to induce malicious or unintended behavior. Rather than simply altering a user's prompt, this type of attack crafts input to leverage the system's broader state and external interactions to bypass safety measures.

| Sub-technique | Name | Definition |
|---|---|---|
| `AISubtech-11.1.1` | Agent-Specific Evasion | Crafting inputs that exploit unique behaviors, roles, or processing patterns of specific agent types (retriever, planner, verifier, executor) to evade detection by some agents while achieving malicious objectives through others. An example: A payload ignored by a reasoning agent but misinterpreted as valid commands by a retriever agent. |
| `AISubtech-11.1.2` | Tool-Scoped Evasion | Payloads crafted to avoid detection by security tools or external components while manifesting malicious behavior when routed to specific vulnerable tools or APIs in the workflow. (An example: A string harmless in chat but which triggers a file-system exploit when passed into a file I/O tool.) |
| `AISubtech-11.1.3` | Environment-Scoped Payloads | Malicious inputs that activate only in specific runtime environments (dev vs. prod, cloud vs. on-prem, specific OS) by checking environment variables, debug flags, or system characteristics before executing. An example: payload checks for debug flags or environment variables before running malicious logic. |
| `AISubtech-11.1.4` | Defense-Aware Payloads | Adversarial payloads explicitly crafted with knowledge of existing defensive mechanisms (prompt constraints, verification steps, content filters) that adapt to evade those specific defenses. |

### AITech-11.2 Model-Selective Evasion

Actors craft prompts or inputs specifically designed to bypass the safety controls, content filters, or detection mechanisms of a particular target LLM, while similar or related models would successfully detect and refuse the malicious input. This technique exploits model-specific quirks, training differences, and implementation variations.

| Sub-technique | Name | Definition |
|---|---|---|
| `AISubtech-11.2.1` | Targeted Model Fingerprinting | Probing, testing, or analyzing a model to determine its specific identity, version, fine-tuning status, or architecture characteristics, enabling attackers to craft model-specific exploits. |
| `AISubtech-11.2.2` | Conditional Attack Execution | Payloads designed to remain benign across most models but trigger harmful actions specifically on targeted models due to differences in tokenization, instruction-following, or training data. An example: An adversarial prompt that looks neutral to one model but forces another into generating malicious output due to differences in tokenizer or instruction-following behavior. |

## OB-012 Action-Space and Integration Abuse

Actors abuse connected tools, APIs, functions, or external capabilities through subversive prompts, commands, or context manipulation. This can include attacks like: unauthorized tool execution, exploitation of security vulnerabilities in tools, tool poisoning, injection attacks through tool interfaces.

### AITech-12.1 Tool Exploitation

Actors abuse connected tools, APIs, functions, or external capabilities through subversive prompts, commands, or context manipulation. This can include attacks like: unauthorized tool execution, exploitation of security vulnerabilities in tools, tool poisoning, injection attacks through tool interfaces.

| Sub-technique | Name | Definition |
|---|---|---|
| `AISubtech-12.1.1` | Parameter Manipulation | Altering, modifying, or manipulating function/tool parameters, model settings, or configuration values to unlock unintended capabilities, bypass restrictions, or enable malicious functionality. |
| `AISubtech-12.1.2` | Tool Poisoning | Corrupting, modifying, or degrading the functionality, outputs, or behavior of tools used by agents through data poisoning, configuration tampering, or behavioral manipulation, causing the tool resulting in deceptive or malicious outputs, privilege escalation, or propagation of altered data. |
| `AISubtech-12.1.3` | Unsafe System / Browser / File Execution | Abusing agentic system integration with system commands, browsers, or file I/O tools to trigger unsafe operations, arbitrary code executions, or malicious file actions. An example: A prompt that tricks an agent into opening arbitrary URLs in a browser tool, leading to drive-by downloads. |
| `AISubtech-12.1.4` | Tool Shadowing | Disguising, substituting or duplicating legitimate tools within an agent or MCP server or tool registry, enabling malicious tools with identical or similar identifiers to intercept or replace trusted tool calls, leading to unauthorized actions, data exfiltration, or redirection of legitimate operations. |

### AITech-12.2 Insecure Output Handling

Actors exploit insufficient sanitization, validation, filtering, or security controls applied to content generated by models or agents before it is passed to downstream systems, databases, APIs, or components. This inadequate handling enables injection attacks, code execution, or broader system compromise.

| Sub-technique | Name | Definition |
|---|---|---|
| `AISubtech-12.2.1` | Code Detection / Malicious Code Output | Forcing an LLM/agent to produce code that bypasses content filters, contains malicious functionality, or includes working exploits, often disguised as benign snippets or requested features. An example: Requesting "educational" shellcode generation that produces working exploits. |

## OB-013 Availability Abuse

Actors prevent authorized users from accessing or using AI models, agents, or their services through resource exhaustion, system degradation, or complete service outage.

### AITech-13.1 Disruption of Availability

Actors prevent authorized users from accessing or using AI models, agents, or their services through resource exhaustion, system degradation, or complete service outage.

| Sub-technique | Name | Definition |
|---|---|---|
| `AISubtech-13.1.1` | Compute Exhaustion | Deliberately consuming excessive computational resources through long queries, adversarial inputs, or compute-intensive requests designed to degrade service availability, increase operational costs, or cause system slowdown. |
| `AISubtech-13.1.2` | Memory Flooding | Overwhelming or overloading the model/agent's memory, API, or processing pipelines with excessive tool calls, simultaneous operations, or memory-intensive requests to degrade performance, cause failures, or erode memory systems. |
| `AISubtech-13.1.3` | Model Denial of Service | An attack designed to degrade or shut down a model or application by flooding the system with requests, requesting large responses, exploiting a vulnerability, or triggering resource-intensive operations. |
| `AISubtech-13.1.4` | Application Denial of Service | Interacting with a model or agent n a method that consumes an exceptionally high amount of resources, resulting degraded service quality for users, as well as potentially incurring high resource costs. |
| `AISubtech-13.1.5` | Decision Paralysis Attacks | Overwhelming model/agent decision-making systems with contradictory information, excessive options, conflicting objectives, or computationally intractable choices to prevent timely decisions, cause system freezing, or force default/unsafe behaviors. |

### AITech-13.2 Cost Harvesting / Repurposing

Actors leverage computational or memory attacks that exploit AI systems to generate excessive costs for the service provider or owner through resource abuse, unauthorized usage for attacker benefit, or deliberate cost inflation. Examples can incude overwhelming human-in-the-loop processes and other denial of service conditions.

| Sub-technique | Name | Definition |
|---|---|---|
| `AISubtech-13.2.1` | Service Misuse for Cost Inflation | The intentional or unintentional use of AI resources in a way that unnecessarily drives up operational costs through inefficient queries, resource waste, or exploitation of usage-based pricing. |

## OB-014 Privilege Compromise

Actors gain unauthorized access to the underlying infrastructure, deployment environment, or hosting systems of AI models and agents (e.g., servers, databases, cloud accounts). This is distinct from accessing the model/agentic system itself through exploitation.

### AITech-14.1 Unauthorized Access

Actors gain unauthorized access to the underlying infrastructure, deployment environment, or hosting systems of AI models and agents (e.g., servers, databases, cloud accounts). This is distinct from accessing the model/agentic system itself through exploitation.

| Sub-technique | Name | Definition |
|---|---|---|
| `AISubtech-14.1.1` | Credential Theft | Attempts to generate, solicit, or reveal authorization credentials (login details, tokens, API keys, passwords) through interactions with model/agent, enabling unauthorized access to accounts, systems, and data. |
| `AISubtech-14.1.2` | Insufficient Access Controls | Weak, missing, or misconfigured permissions, authentication mechanisms, and access measures that fail to adequately prevent security breaches, unauthorized access, or data leakage. |

### AITech-14.2 Abuse of Delegated Authority

Actors exploit legitimate delegation mechanisms where agents are granted authority to act on behalf of users, systems, or other agents, and use this delegated authority to perform unauthorized actions, exceed intended scope, or abuse trust relationships for malicious purposes.

| Sub-technique | Name | Definition |
|---|---|---|
| `AISubtech-14.2.1` | Permission Escalation via Delegation | Action that exceeds the scope or resource access initially allowed to a subject or user, exploiting delegation mechanisms to gain privileged access and perform unauthorized tasks beyond original authorization. |

## OB-015 Harmful / Misleading / Inaccurate Content

Actors prompt generative models or agents to produce unauthorized, unsafe, or malicious content, including harmful instructions, toxic speech, misinformation, or unsafe media. The attack targets weaknesses in content guardrails to bypass safety constraints and generate content that should otherwise be restricted.

### AITech-15.1 Harmful Content

Actors prompt generative models or agents to produce unauthorized, unsafe, or malicious content, including harmful instructions, toxic speech, misinformation, or unsafe media. The attack targets weaknesses in content guardrails to bypass safety constraints and generate content that should otherwise be restricted.

| Sub-technique | Name | Definition |
|---|---|---|
| `AISubtech-15.1.1` | Cybersecurity and Hacking: Malware / Exploits | Prompts, content, or outputs, whether expressed as text, audio, visual material, actions, operations, or other modes from LLMs (as well as the use of agentic AI systems, their components, or elements) that enable or facilitate the creation, distribution, or operational use of malicious software and related cyberattack activities. This may include generating code, instructions, or automation that produces or deploys malware, viruses, or exploits; orchestrating network intrusions or ransomware campaigns; and managing malicious infrastructure.<br>Examples of malware, viruses and exploits:<br>• Software designed to covertly monitor user activity, display unsolicited advertisements, collect personal data without consent, or provide misleading functionality.<br>• Adware, spyware, stalkerware, potentially unwanted applications (PUAs).<br>Agentic capabilities and components may also be abused to coordinate attacks, automate vulnerability exploitation, or assist in the trade and resale of compromised assets, scaling cyber threats far beyond traditional manual hacking operations. |
| `AISubtech-15.1.2` | Cybersecurity and Hacking: Cyber Abuse | Prompts, content, or outputs, whether expressed as text, audio, visual material, actions, operations, or other modes from LLMs (as well as the use of agentic AI systems, their components, or elements) that enable or facilitate attacks in which actors manipulate human trust, behavior, or decision-making to gain unauthorized access, extract sensitive data, or cause harmful actions.<br>This may include or facilitate:<br>• Hacking<br>• Ransomware operations<br>• Network attack operations<br>• Malicious infrastructure operations<br>• Compromised asset trading<br>• Phishing<br>• Social engineering (convincing malicious communications such as phishing emails, spoofed chat messages, or voice calls)<br>Agentic systems and their components may be abused to scale, personalize, and automate social engineering campaigns far beyond traditional human-driven methods, such as deploying automated conversational or task-driven agents designed to deceive targets. |

| `AISubtech-15.1.4` | Safety Harms and Toxicity: Child Abuse / Exploitation | Prompts, content, or outputs, whether expressed as text, audio, visual material, actions, operations, or other modes from LLMs (as well as the use of agentic AI systems, their components, or elements) that intend to enable harm and malice against children, especially in exploiting them physically or emotionally.<br>This may include intentionally tampering with children's images and inciting nudity, child pornography or directly encouraging violence against children. |

## OB-016 Surveillance

Actors conduct unauthorized passive monitoring, interception, or extraction of data from model/agentic system communications, including agent-to-agent messages, agent-to-user interactions, API calls, or other internal communications without directly manipulating the data flow.

### AITech-16.1 Eavesdropping

Actors conduct unauthorized passive monitoring, interception, or extraction of data from model/agentic system communications, including agent-to-agent messages, agent-to-user interactions, API calls, or other internal communications without directly manipulating the data flow.

| Sub-technique | Name | Definition |
|---|---|---|
| `AISubtech-16.1.1` | Logging Sensitive Conversations | Storing or recording user-model interactions in ways that include personally identifiable information (PII), private data, or sensitive content, without adequate consent, anonymization, security, or retention limits (which could eventually be leaked or misused). |

## OB-017 Cyber-Physical / Sensor Attacks

Actors use of highly-realistic but deceptive signals or manipulating sensor data to deliberately mislead an AI system and its decision-making processes through falsified sensory inputs.

### AITech-17.1 Sensor Spoofing

Actors use of highly-realistic but deceptive signals or manipulating sensor data to deliberately mislead an AI system and its decision-making processes through falsified sensory inputs.

| Sub-technique | Name | Definition |
|---|---|---|
| `AISubtech-17.1.1` | Sensor Spoofing: Action Signals (audio, visual) | Data points or signals that prompt a model to undertake specific actions beyond reasoning. These signals can be malicious or benign, allowing agents to execute operations in physical or digital environments. |

## OB-018 System Misuse / Malicious Application

Actors leverage models/agents specifically for generating, executing, scaling, or automating fraud, scams, deception, and other illegal activities.

### AITech-18.1 Fraudulent Use

Actors leverage models/agents specifically for generating, executing, scaling, or automating fraud, scams, deception, and other illegal activities.

| Sub-technique | Name | Definition |
|---|---|---|
| `AISubtech-18.1.1` | Spam / Scam / Social Engineering Generation | Automating generation of large volumes of unsolicited or fraudulent content (phishing, fake offers, spam emails/messages, impersonation or manipulation of trust) to deceive people or solicit funds, credentials, personal and confidential information, or other valuables. |

### AITech-18.2 Malicious Workflows

Actors leverage AI models to generate, execute, and scale harmful activities like cyberattacks, data theft, and disinformation campaigns. among other deceptive purposes.

| Sub-technique | Name | Definition |
|---|---|---|
| `AISubtech-18.2.1` | Abuse of APIs for Mass Automation | Leveraging APIs in bulk for malicious purpose at scale, including flooding attacks, automation of worst-case prompts, or executing workflows that negatively impact many users or systems. |
| `AISubtech-18.2.2` | Dedicated Malicious Server or Infrastructure | Establishing purpose-built servers, infrastructure, or services specifically designed to support, scale, or automate AI-powered attacks, malicious workflows, or harmful operations. |

## OB-019 Multimodal / Cross-Modal Risks

Actors exploit contradictions, mismatches, or inconsistencies between different data modalities (i.e., text, image, audio, video) to confuse AI systems, bypass security controls, evade detection, or manipulate decision-making by presenting conflicting information across modalities that the system cannot properly reconcile.

### AITech-19.1 Cross-Modal Inconsistency Exploits

Actors exploit contradictions, mismatches, or inconsistencies between different data modalities (i.e., text, image, audio, video) to confuse AI systems, bypass security controls, evade detection, or manipulate decision-making by presenting conflicting information across modalities that the system cannot properly reconcile.

| Sub-technique | Name | Definition |
|---|---|---|
| `AISubtech-19.1.1` | Contradictory Inputs Attack | Exploiting a model's inability to consistently handle conflicting instructions by embedding deceptive or contradictory commands within user input across or within modalities, causing behavior drift toward malicious objectives. |
| `AISubtech-19.1.2` | Modality Skewing | Manipulating one modality (e.g., corrupting audio transcript, poisoning image metadata) to bias arbitration mechanisms toward favoring the manipulated channel over others. |

### AITech-19.2 Fusion Payload Split

Actors exploit weaknesses in fusion algorithms, arbitration logic, and decision-making processes to manipulate final system behavior. Combining payload components delivered through different inputs, outputs, or sources (including data sources, multiple models, or agents) and using the system’s fusion or arbitration mechanisms to assemble them to create an injection or attack payload.

| Sub-technique | Name | Definition |
|---|---|---|
| `AISubtech-19.2.1` | Convergence Payload Injection | Injecting adversarial data into training or other data sources across any modality to corrupt joint embeddings or fusion layers and establish a hidden payload that can later be activated. One part of the payload is embedded during data poisoning, while the other part is delivered at runtime. These components are combined to produces an attack or injection payload. |
| `AISubtech-19.2.2` | Chained Payload Execution | Crafting partial or complementary payload components across any modality, source, or agent output that, when fused by the system, contribute to producing an attack. Both parts of the payload are delivered at runtime, and when the system combines these components through its fusion or arbitration mechanisms, they form an attack or injection payload. |
